category: Flat adverbs: the same form as the adjective

examples: Don't talk so fast — I can't follow you.
She ran faster than anyone else on the team.
Prices are rising fast this year.
The truck was stuck fast in the mud.
Hold fast to the railing when the boat turns.
The senator stood fast and refused to change her vote.
By nine o'clock the kids were fast asleep.
He was so fast asleep that he didn't hear the alarm.
The clock in the kitchen runs five minutes fast.
My watch has been running fast ever since I dropped it.

senses.head: Quickly; at high speed
examples: Don't talk so fast — I can't follow you.
She ran faster than anyone else on the team.
Prices are rising fast this year.

senses.head: Firmly, so that it cannot move or come loose
examples: The truck was stuck fast in the mud.
Hold fast to the railing when the boat turns.
The senator stood fast and refused to change her vote.

senses.head: Deeply, in fast asleep
examples: By nine o'clock the kids were fast asleep.
He was so fast asleep that he didn't hear the alarm.

senses.head: Ahead of the correct time, of a clock or watch
examples: The clock in the kitchen runs five minutes fast.
My watch has been running fast ever since I dropped it.

entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective fast; there is no fastly
entries.contrast: There is no fastly: He drives fast, never He drives fastly. The old sense 'firmly' survives in set phrases and has nothing to do with speed: hold fast means hold on tight, stuck fast means it will not move, and fast asleep means deeply asleep, not that someone fell asleep quickly.

Turn the wheel hard to the right.
The pilot banked hard left to avoid the storm.
The second storm came hard on the heels of the first.
The announcement came hard on the heels of a bad quarter.

senses.head: With a lot of effort, energy or attention
examples: She worked hard to pay off her student loans.
Think hard before you sign that contract.
If you try harder, you'll make the team next year.

senses.head: With force; strongly or heavily
examples: It was raining hard when we left.
He hit the ball hard toward left field.
Press hard on the cut to stop the bleeding.

senses.head: With pain or distress, about news or a loss
examples: She took her father's death very hard.
Don't take it so hard — everyone fails a test sometimes.

senses.head: Closely following; right after, in hard on the heels of

entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective hard; hardly is a different word
entries.contrast: Hardly is not the adverb of hard in meaning: it means 'almost not' (group 3). She works hard = она много работает; She hardly works = она почти не работает. Russian тяжело about bad news is also hard: He took it hard.

examples: The train got in forty minutes late.

senses.head: After the expected, usual or proper time
examples: The train got in forty minutes late.
Sorry, I'm running late — start without me.
She stayed later than everyone else to finish the report.

senses.head: Near the end of a period of time
examples: The accident happened late at night.
He started painting late in life.
The package should arrive late next week.

senses.head: Recently, in as late as and of late
examples: As late as 2010, the town had no traffic lights.
The house was lived in until as late as the 1980s.
The senator has been unusually quiet of late.

entries.position: end — after the verb or its object; before in, at, next in late at night
entries.modifies: verbs; time phrases (late in the day)
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective late
entries.contrast: Lately is a different word: it means 'recently, в последнее время' (group 3). I got home late = я поздно пришёл домой; I haven't slept well lately = в последнее время я плохо сплю. Later meaning 'afterward' (See you later) is a time adverb of its own (group 6).

examples: We got to the airport two hours early.

Early in her career, she worked as a waitress.

senses.head: Before the usual, expected or planned time
examples: We got to the airport two hours early.
The baby was born three weeks early.
Can you come in earlier tomorrow?

senses.head: Near the beginning of a period of time
examples: I get up early in the morning.
Early in her career, she worked as a waitress.
We knew early on that the plan wouldn't work.

entries.position: end — after the verb or its object; before in, on in early in the morning
entries.modifies: verbs; time phrases (early in the year)
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective early; the -ly is part of the word, so there is no earlily
entries.contrast: Early is about the clock or calendar — before the usual time (рано, раньше срока); soon is about how long from now (скоро). Come early = приходите пораньше; Come soon = приходите поскорее. Russian раньше meaning 'in the past' is before or used to, not earlier: I used to smoke. Earlier meaning 'ранее, сегодня уже' (I called you earlier) has its own entry (group 6).

examples: Go straight for two blocks and turn left at the light.
Sit up straight and look at the camera.

examples: I went straight home after work.

senses.head: Honestly; without hiding anything, or, in go straight, without breaking the law
examples: Just tell me straight — am I getting fired?
I'll give it to you straight: the car isn't worth fixing.
After prison he went straight and opened a bakery.

senses.head: Without a break; in a row, after a number and a time word
examples: It rained for five days straight.
The Yankees have won six games straight.

senses.head: Clearly, in think straight and see straight
examples: I'm so tired I can't think straight.
After three drinks he couldn't see straight.

senses.head: Without water, ice or anything mixed in, of a drink
examples: He drinks his whiskey straight.
Do you want your bourbon straight or on the rocks?

entries.type: manner; also direction, time (straight home) and duration (three days straight)
entries.position: end — after the verb; before home, ahead, to; after a time phrase in three days straight
entries.comparison: -er/-est — straighter, straightest; only in the line and posture sense
entries.modifies: verbs; place words (straight ahead); time phrases (five days straight)
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective straight; straightly is almost never used
entries.contrast: Russian прямо as an intensifier is right, not straight: прямо сейчас = right now, прямо здесь = right here. Straight means in a line, without stopping, or honestly: go straight home. Straight away (сразу) is heard in the US, but right away is far more common.

examples: Have you been waiting long?

senses.head: For a long time
examples: Have you been waiting long?
It won't take long to fix.
Can you stay a little longer?

senses.head: A long time before or after a point, or for a long time up to now
examples: The house was built long ago.
We were friends long before we started dating.
Scientists have long suspected a link between the two.

senses.head: Throughout a whole period, in all day long, all year long
examples: The baby cried all night long.
The pool is open all summer long.

senses.head: Any more, in no longer and not any longer
examples: She no longer works here.
I can't wait any longer.

entries.position: end — Did you wait long?; mid in have long suspected; before ago, before, after
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective long
entries.contrast: In affirmative statements American English says a long time, not bare long: I waited a long time, not I waited long. Bare long is normal in questions and negatives (Did you wait long?, It won't take long) and after too, so, as (I stayed too long). Long is about time; for distance use far or a long way — sports talk is the exception (throw long, the putt went long). As long as (если только; пока) is a conjunction.

senses.head: At a high level, rank, amount or pitch

entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective high
entries.contrast: Highly does not mean 'at a great height': it means 'very' or 'very well' (highly recommended, think highly of — group 3). The kite flew high, never flew highly; a highly successful company, never a high successful company.

senses.head: At a low level, amount, price or setting

entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective low
entries.contrast: Lowly is an adjective meaning 'humble, of low rank' (a lowly clerk), not the adverb of low. Lower is also a verb: Lower your voice = говорите тише.

examples: The roots go deep into the soil.
They hiked deeper into the woods.
The quarterback threw deep to the end zone.

senses.head: Far into a period of time
examples: We talked deep into the night.
The game went deep into overtime.

senses.head: At a deep level of feeling or effort, in dig deep and run deep
examples: The team had to dig deep to win in the final minutes.
Old grudges run deep in this town.

entries.type: place; also time (deep into the night) and degree
entries.position: end — after the verb; before into, under phrases
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective deep
entries.contrast: For feelings and degree use deeply: deeply sorry, deeply moved, I deeply regret it — never deep sorry (group 3). Flat deep is for physical depth or distance and a few set phrases: dig deep, deep into the night, run deep. With breathe both work: breathe deep, breathe deeply.

examples: Don't come any nearer — the dog bites.
As the wedding drew near, she got more nervous.
The deer came near enough to eat from my hand.
It was near impossible to find parking.
The team played a near perfect game.

senses.head: At or to a short distance in space or time
examples: Don't come any nearer — the dog bites.
As the wedding drew near, she got more nervous.
The deer came near enough to eat from my hand.

senses.head: Almost; very nearly, informal, before an adjective
examples: It was near impossible to find parking.
The team played a near perfect game.

senses.head: Not at all, in nowhere near and not anywhere near
examples: The house is nowhere near finished.
We don't have anywhere near enough chairs.

entries.type: place; also time and degree (near perfect)
entries.position: end — after the verb; before its word in near perfect
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective near
entries.contrast: Near is usually a preposition (near the station); it is an adverb only when no noun follows (come near). For location, everyday American speech prefers nearby: They live nearby. For 'almost', formal writing uses nearly (group 3): nearly impossible, not near impossible. Nowhere near (далеко не) is informal but standard.

So far, nobody has complained.
Thus far the plan is working.
The party went on far into the night.
Her family's roots go as far back as the 1700s.

senses.head: At or to a great distance
examples: How far is the airport from here?
They don't live far from us.
We drove farther than we'd planned.

senses.head: Much; by a large amount, before a comparative or too, and in by far
examples: This version is far better than the last one.
The rent is far too high.
She's by far the best player on the team.

senses.head: To a particular point, degree or stage
examples: How far did you get with the reading?
This time he's gone too far.
As far as I know, the store is still open.

senses.head: Up to now, in so far and thus far
examples: So far, nobody has complained.
Thus far the plan is working.

senses.head: A long way in time, before into, back and ahead
examples: The party went on far into the night.
Her family's roots go as far back as the 1700s.
It's too early to plan that far ahead.

entries.type: place; also degree (far better) and time (so far)
entries.position: end — after the verb; before its word in far better, far too
entries.comparison: irregular — farther, farthest; also further, furthest
entries.modifies: verbs; comparatives and too (far better, far too)
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective far; compares irregularly
entries.contrast: In affirmative statements bare far sounds formal; Americans say a long way: We walked a long way. Far is normal in questions and negatives (Is it far?, It's not far) and with too, so, away, from. Before a comparative use far or much, never very: far better, not very better. Far from + adjective means 'not at all': far from perfect = далеко не идеальный. For distance American English prefers farther; further also means 'more, in addition' (group 2).

examples: You spelled my name wrong.
I guessed wrong about the weather.
Don't get me wrong — I like her a lot.
Something went wrong with the engine.
What could possibly go wrong?
Where did we go wrong with this project?

senses.head: Incorrectly; in a mistaken way
examples: You spelled my name wrong.
I guessed wrong about the weather.
Don't get me wrong — I like her a lot.

senses.head: Badly, so that a problem happens, in go wrong
examples: Something went wrong with the engine.
What could possibly go wrong?
Where did we go wrong with this project?

entries.position: end — only after the verb or its object
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective wrong
entries.contrast: Flat wrong goes only after the verb or object: You spelled it wrong. Before a verb or participle use wrongly: He was wrongly accused. Wrongly also carries the idea of 'unfairly, by mistake' (group 3). Don't get me wrong = не поймите меня неправильно.

Hold on, I'll be right back.

Did I pronounce that right?

If I remember right, the party starts at eight.
The nail went right through the board.
Read the contract right to the end.
He turned right around and walked out.
Turn right at the second light.
Look left and right before you cross.

senses.head: Exactly; directly, before a place or time word
examples: The keys were right here on the table.
She was sitting right in front of me.
Call me right after the meeting.

senses.head: Immediately; without delay, in right away, right now, right back
examples: I need those files right away.
Hold on, I'll be right back.
Stop that right now!

senses.head: Correctly; as it should be
examples: Did I pronounce that right?
Nothing is going right today.
If I remember right, the party starts at eight.

senses.head: All the way; completely
examples: The nail went right through the board.
Read the contract right to the end.
He turned right around and walked out.

senses.head: To or toward the right side
examples: Turn right at the second light.
Look left and right before you cross.

entries.type: focusing; also time (right away), manner (do it right), degree (right to the end) and direction (turn right)
entries.position: before its word — right here, right after lunch; end in do it right, turn right
entries.modifies: place and time words and phrases; verbs
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective right
entries.contrast: Russian прямо before a place or time word is right, not straight: right now, right here, right in front of you. Right now means 'at this moment'; just now means 'a moment ago'. Rightly (group 3) means 'justifiably': She was rightly proud; You guessed right uses the flat form. Right? at the end of a sentence is a question tag, and Right. alone is an interjection.

examples: You can fly direct from Chicago to Tokyo.
This bus goes direct to the airport.
We buy our coffee direct from the farmers.
If there's a problem, contact me direct.
The payment goes direct into your account.

senses.head: Without stopping or changing along the way
examples: You can fly direct from Chicago to Tokyo.
This bus goes direct to the airport.

senses.head: Without anyone or anything in between
examples: We buy our coffee direct from the farmers.
If there's a problem, contact me direct.
The payment goes direct into your account.

entries.position: end — after the verb (fly direct, buy direct)
entries.modifies: verbs of travel, buying and contact
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective direct
entries.contrast: Flat direct is used mainly after verbs of travel and dealing: fly direct, buy direct, call direct. Directly covers everything else and is the only choice before an adjective or verb: directly affected, directly opposite. Directly can also mean 'very soon' (I'll be there directly, older and Southern US). Both /dəˈrɛkt/ and /daɪˈrɛkt/ are standard American pronunciations.

entries.meaning: According to the rules; honestly and without cheating. ---
examples: You have to play fair, even when you're losing.
They won the election fair and square.
Couples therapy taught them how to fight fair.
entries.position: end — after the verb (play fair)
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective fair
entries.contrast: Flat fair lives in a few phrases: play fair, fight fair, fair and square. Elsewhere use fairly, which usually means 'rather' (fairly good = довольно хороший) and only sometimes 'justly' (treat people fairly) — group 3. Russian честно говоря is honestly or to be fair, not fair.

examples: Children under five ride free.

Seniors get in free on Tuesdays.
The dog pulled free of its leash.
She finally broke free of the crowd.
Wild horses run free on the island.

senses.head: Without payment
examples: Children under five ride free.
I got these tickets free from work.
Seniors get in free on Tuesdays.

senses.head: Out of a hold or away from a restraint; loose
examples: The dog pulled free of its leash.
She finally broke free of the crowd.
Wild horses run free on the island.

entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective free
entries.contrast: Free after a verb means 'for no money': Kids eat free. Freely means 'without limits or control': speak freely (говорить открыто), freely available (group 3). Russian свободно говорить по-английски is speak English fluently, not freely. For free is informal but normal in American English; free of charge is formal.

senses.head: Fully; to the full extent
examples: Open wider, please — I can't see the tooth.
The front door was wide open.
At three in the morning I was still wide awake.

senses.head: Away from the target; off to one side
examples: His kick went wide, and the game ended in a tie.
The shot sailed wide of the net.

senses.head: Over a large area, in far and wide
examples: People came from far and wide to hear her speak.
The news spread far and wide.

entries.position: end — open wide; before its word in wide open, wide awake
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective wide
entries.contrast: Flat wide is physical: open wide, wide open, wide awake. For how many people or how much, use widely: widely known, widely used, prices vary widely — never wide known (group 3). Wide open can also mean 'undecided': The race is wide open.

examples: Stay close to me in the crowd.
Come closer so I can see you.
She held the baby close and rocked him to sleep.
Close to 500 people showed up.
I came close to quitting last year.
It was close to midnight when they got home.
Listen close, because I'm only saying this once.
Watch close and you'll see how he does the trick.

senses.head: Near in space or time
examples: Stay close to me in the crowd.
Come closer so I can see you.
She held the baby close and rocked him to sleep.

senses.head: Almost; nearly, in close to + a number or time and come close
examples: Close to 500 people showed up.
I came close to quitting last year.
It was close to midnight when they got home.

senses.head: Carefully; with attention, informal
examples: Listen close, because I'm only saying this once.
Watch close and you'll see how he does the trick.

entries.type: place; also degree (close to 500) and manner (listen close)
entries.position: end — after the verb; before to, by, behind
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective close
entries.contrast: The adverb and adjective close end in /s/: /kloʊs/. The verb close ends in /z/: /kloʊz/. Closely means 'carefully' or 'in a close relationship': watch closely, closely related (group 3); flat close is mainly physical distance: stand close. Close to + a number means 'almost': close to 500.

examples: The ball landed short of the green.

senses.head: Before reaching a goal, target or amount, in fall short and come up short
examples: The ball landed short of the green.
Sales fell short of expectations.
Our team came up short in the final round.

senses.head: Suddenly and abruptly, in stop short and pull up short
examples: She stopped short when she saw the snake.
The driver pulled up short at the crosswalk.

senses.head: Earlier than planned, in cut short
examples: We had to cut our vacation short.
His career was cut short by a knee injury.

senses.head: Below its real worth, in sell short
examples: Don't sell yourself short — you're great at this.
Critics sold the movie short, but it became a hit.

entries.position: end — after the verb or its object (stop short, cut it short)
entries.modifies: verbs (fall, come up, stop, cut, sell)
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective short
entries.contrast: Shortly means 'soon' (скоро): I'll be there shortly (group 3) — it has nothing to do with length. Short of works like a preposition meaning 'except, without going as far as': Short of a miracle, we'll lose. In short (короче говоря) is a linking phrase.

examples: 'Can I borrow your pen?' 'Sure, go ahead.'
Sure, I'll give you a ride.
'Want to grab lunch?' 'Sure.'
It sure is hot today.
I sure hope they win.
You sure know how to throw a party.
Sure, it's expensive, but it'll last twenty years.
The job pays well, sure, but the hours are terrible.
'Thanks for the help.' 'Sure.'
'Thanks for waiting.' 'Oh, sure, no problem.'
I said it would rain, and sure enough, it did.
Sure enough, the store was closed when we got there.

senses.head: Yes; certainly, as a reply or agreement
examples: 'Can I borrow your pen?' 'Sure, go ahead.'
Sure, I'll give you a ride.
'Want to grab lunch?' 'Sure.'

senses.head: Really; certainly, for emphasis before the verb
examples: It sure is hot today.
I sure hope they win.
You sure know how to throw a party.

senses.head: Admittedly, before a but
examples: Sure, it's expensive, but it'll last twenty years.
The job pays well, sure, but the hours are terrible.

senses.head: You're welcome, in reply to thanks
examples: 'Thanks for the help.' 'Sure.'
'Thanks for waiting.' 'Oh, sure, no problem.'

senses.head: As expected, in sure enough
examples: I said it would rain, and sure enough, it did.
Sure enough, the store was closed when we got there.

entries.type: stance; also degree (It sure is hot)
entries.position: front — alone as a reply or before a clause; mid in It sure is hot
entries.contrast: Adverb sure is informal American English; in writing use certainly. Surely is not a neutral 'certainly': Surely you're not serious? expresses surprise or disbelief — неужели, не может быть (group 3). For sure (наверняка) is a set phrase: I don't know for sure. I'm sure is the adjective.

examples: Come quick — the kitchen's on fire!
Nobody gets rich quick by playing the lottery.
Take the highway — you'll get there quicker.
entries.position: end — after the verb; never before the verb
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective quick; the regular adverb is quickly
entries.contrast: Flat quick is informal and mostly appears after the verb in commands and set phrases: Come quick!, get rich quick. Before the verb only quickly works: She quickly agreed, never She quick agreed. The comparative quicker is normal even in careful speech: You'll get there quicker.

examples: Drive slow — the roads are icy.
Let's take it slow and see how things go.
Could you talk a little slower?
The clock in the hallway runs ten minutes slow.
My watch is running slow again.

senses.head: Slowly; at low speed
examples: Drive slow — the roads are icy.
Let's take it slow and see how things go.
Could you talk a little slower?

senses.head: Behind the correct time, of a clock or watch
examples: The clock in the hallway runs ten minutes slow.
My watch is running slow again.

entries.position: end — after the verb; never before the verb
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective slow; the regular adverb is slowly
entries.contrast: Flat slow is informal outside a few uses: go slow, drive slow, take it slow and the road sign SLOW. In writing and before the verb use slowly: She slowly opened the door. Slower and more slowly are both fine.

examples: Can you talk louder? I can't hear you.
The band played so loud our ears were ringing.
Our neighbors play their music way too loud.
Read the first paragraph out loud, please.
Sorry, I was just thinking out loud.

senses.head: Loudly; with a lot of sound
examples: Can you talk louder? I can't hear you.
The band played so loud our ears were ringing.
Our neighbors play their music way too loud.

senses.head: Aloud, so that others can hear, in out loud
examples: Read the first paragraph out loud, please.
Sorry, I was just thinking out loud.
She laughed out loud at the email.

entries.position: end — after the verb; never before the verb
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective loud; the regular adverb is loudly
entries.contrast: Out loud means 'вслух' — so that others can hear — not 'громко': you can read out loud in a quiet voice. Aloud is the formal equivalent. Before the verb use loudly: He loudly complained. Louder and more loudly are both correct.

examples: Hold on tight — the road gets bumpy.
He squeezed her hand tighter.
Good night, sleep tight!
Sit tight — the doctor will be with you in a minute.
Hang tight, we're almost there.

senses.head: Firmly; closely, so there is no space or movement
examples: Hold on tight — the road gets bumpy.
He squeezed her hand tighter.
Good night, sleep tight!

senses.head: Without moving or acting; patiently, in sit tight and hang tight
examples: Sit tight — the doctor will be with you in a minute.
Hang tight, we're almost there.

entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective tight; the regular adverb is tightly
entries.contrast: Flat tight follows the verb: hold tight, shut tight, packed tight. Before a verb or participle use tightly: tightly packed, She tightly gripped the rail. Sit tight and hang tight do not describe how you sit or hang — they mean 'wait patiently'.

examples: I got this jacket cheap at a thrift store.
Good lawyers don't come cheap.
You can find the same TV cheaper online.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.modifies: verbs of buying, selling and getting
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective cheap; the regular adverb is cheaply
entries.contrast: Flat cheap goes only with verbs of buying, selling and getting: buy cheap, sell it cheap, doesn't come cheap. Cheaply describes how something is done and often sounds negative: cheaply made = дёшево и некачественно сделанный.

examples: The doctor told him to take it easy for a week.
You can rest easy — the kids are safe.
Now that the loan is paid off, we can breathe easier.
Go easy on him — it's his first day.
Go easy on the salt.
That's easier said than done.
Money never came easy for their family.
Easy come, easy go.

senses.head: In a relaxed way, without worry or effort, in take it easy, rest easy, breathe easy
examples: The doctor told him to take it easy for a week.
You can rest easy — the kids are safe.
Now that the loan is paid off, we can breathe easier.

senses.head: Gently; not too strictly or heavily, in go easy on
examples: Go easy on him — it's his first day.
Go easy on the salt.

senses.head: Without difficulty, informal
examples: That's easier said than done.
Money never came easy for their family.
Easy come, easy go.

entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective easy; the regular adverb is easily
entries.contrast: With most verbs use easily: She won easily, not won easy. Flat easy lives in set phrases: take it easy, go easy on, rest easy, easier said than done, easy come, easy go. Take it easy is also a casual American goodbye.

examples: The bullet went clean through the door.
The branch snapped clean off.
I clean forgot about your birthday.
Both teams played clean all season.
The old boxer always fought clean.
He finally came clean about the money.
It's time to come clean with your parents.

senses.head: Completely; all the way, informal, before through, off, out of
examples: The bullet went clean through the door.
The branch snapped clean off.
I clean forgot about your birthday.

senses.head: Fairly; by the rules
examples: Both teams played clean all season.
The old boxer always fought clean.

senses.head: Honestly, admitting what you had hidden, in come clean
examples: He finally came clean about the money.
It's time to come clean with your parents.

entries.type: degree — completely (clean through); also manner (play clean)
entries.position: before its word — clean through, clean forgot; end in play clean
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective clean
entries.contrast: Flat clean before a preposition means 'completely': clean through, clean off. Cleanly (group 3) means 'neatly, without mess': The bone broke cleanly. In wipe the table clean the word is an adjective — it describes the table after wiping.

examples: Stand clear of the closing doors.
The driver jumped clear just before the crash.
I'd steer clear of that neighborhood at night.
She drove clear across town to pick me up.
On a good day you can see clear to the mountains.
I hear you loud and clear.
The message came through loud and clear: no more overtime.

senses.head: Away from something; out of the way, not touching
examples: Stand clear of the closing doors.
The driver jumped clear just before the crash.
I'd steer clear of that neighborhood at night.

senses.head: All the way; completely, informal
examples: She drove clear across town to pick me up.
On a good day you can see clear to the mountains.

senses.head: Clearly; distinctly, in loud and clear
examples: I hear you loud and clear.
The message came through loud and clear: no more overtime.

entries.type: place — away (stand clear); also degree (clear across town) and manner (loud and clear)
entries.position: end — stand clear; before its word in clear across town
entries.modifies: verbs; of phrases; place phrases (clear across)
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective clear
entries.contrast: Clearly means 'obviously' or 'distinctly': Clearly, he's lying; speak clearly (group 3). Flat clear means 'away from' (stand clear of the doors) or, informally, 'all the way' (clear across town). Steer clear of = избегать, держаться подальше.

examples: I'm dead serious — don't touch that.
The experts were dead wrong about the election.
By Friday night I was dead tired.
There's a truck dead ahead.
The arrow hit dead center.
Your guess was dead on.
The deer stopped dead in the road.
She stopped dead in her tracks when she saw him.

senses.head: Completely; absolutely, informal, before an adjective
examples: I'm dead serious — don't touch that.
The experts were dead wrong about the election.
By Friday night I was dead tired.

senses.head: Exactly; directly
examples: There's a truck dead ahead.
The arrow hit dead center.
Your guess was dead on.

senses.head: Suddenly and completely, in stop dead
examples: The deer stopped dead in the road.
She stopped dead in her tracks when she saw him.

entries.position: before its word — dead serious, dead ahead; end in stop dead
entries.modifies: a few adjectives (serious, wrong, tired, certain); place words (ahead, center)
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective dead
entries.contrast: In American English dead intensifies only a few words: dead serious, dead wrong, dead tired, dead certain, dead set against. British dead good, dead easy sound foreign to most Americans. Deadly is mainly an adjective (смертельный); deadly serious is close to dead serious.

examples: Wash your hands first.
First, preheat the oven to 350 degrees.
Let me finish my coffee first.
She crossed the finish line first.
You go first — I'll wait.
Safety always comes first.
I first met my wife in college.
When did you first notice the pain?
The song was first recorded in 1965.
Apologize to him? I'd quit first.
Borrow money from him? I'd sleep in my car first.

senses.head: Before doing anything else
examples: Wash your hands first.
First, preheat the oven to 350 degrees.
Let me finish my coffee first.

senses.head: Before all others in order, time or importance
examples: She crossed the finish line first.
You go first — I'll wait.
Safety always comes first.

senses.head: For the first time
examples: I first met my wife in college.
When did you first notice the pain?
The song was first recorded in 1965.

senses.head: Rather; in preference, in refusals
examples: Apologize to him? I'd quit first.
Borrow money from him? I'd sleep in my car first.

entries.position: front or end — First, …; finish first; mid in when we first met
entries.form: flat — the same form as the ordinal and adjective first
entries.contrast: At first means 'at the beginning, before things changed' (поначалу): At first I hated the city, but now I love it. First means 'before anything else' or introduces the first point (сначала, во-первых): First, read the instructions. American English prefers first to firstly (group 3) in lists. First of all = прежде всего.

examples: Our team finished last again.
Add the cheese last so it doesn't burn.
He always arrives first and leaves last.
When did you last see your wallet?
I last spoke to her in March.
The bridge was last repaired in 1998.
Last, I want to thank my parents.
And last but not least, our wonderful volunteers.

senses.head: After all others in order or time
examples: Our team finished last again.
Add the cheese last so it doesn't burn.
He always arrives first and leaves last.

senses.head: Most recently; on the latest occasion
examples: When did you last see your wallet?
I last spoke to her in March.
The bridge was last repaired in 1998.

senses.head: Finally, as the last point in a list
examples: Last, I want to thank my parents.
And last but not least, our wonderful volunteers.

entries.position: end — came last; mid in I last saw; front in Last, …
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective last
entries.contrast: At last means 'finally, after a long wait' (наконец-то): At last we're home! Bare last means 'after everyone else' (последним) or 'the most recent time' (в последний раз). Lastly (group 3) introduces the final point, like last. Russian последний раз is the last time or mid-position last: When did you last see him?

examples: Even a child could do this.

The restaurant was full, even on a Monday.
The second movie was even better than the first.
It's going to get even colder tonight.
The hotel was expensive. Even so, we'd stay there again.
It's a long shot. Even so, it's worth a try.

senses.head: Used to show that something is surprising or more than expected
examples: Even a child could do this.
He didn't even say goodbye.
The restaurant was full, even on a Monday.

senses.head: Still more, before a comparative
examples: The second movie was even better than the first.
It's going to get even colder tonight.

senses.head: In spite of that, in even so
examples: The hotel was expensive. Even so, we'd stay there again.
It's a long shot. Even so, it's worth a try.

entries.type: focusing; also degree (even better) and linking (even so)
entries.position: before its word — the word it focuses on; mid in He didn't even call
entries.modifies: any word or phrase it focuses on; comparatives
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective even (ровный), with a different meaning
entries.contrast: Position changes the meaning: Even Tom laughed (даже Том засмеялся) vs Tom even laughed (Том даже засмеялся). With a comparative, Russian ещё is even, not more: even better, never more better. Even if (даже если) and even though (хотя) are conjunctions, and Russian speakers mix them: Even though it rained, we went — it did rain. Evenly (group 3) means 'equally, smoothly'.

senses.head: Fairly; rather; quite
examples: The movie was pretty good.
I'm pretty sure I locked the door.
She speaks Spanish pretty well.

senses.head: Almost; nearly, in pretty much and pretty well
examples: I'm pretty much done with the project.
That's pretty much all I know.
The storm pretty well destroyed the barn.

senses.head: In a good or comfortable position, in sitting pretty
examples: With two job offers, she's sitting pretty.
If the stock keeps rising, we'll be sitting pretty.

entries.position: before its word — adjectives and adverbs
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective pretty (красивый), but unrelated in meaning
entries.contrast: The adverb has nothing to do with beauty: pretty ugly = довольно уродливый. It is weaker than very and very common in American speech, less so in formal writing. Pretty good often means only 'OK'. Prettily (group 3) means 'in a pretty way'.

senses.head: Only; simply; no more than
examples: It's just a game — relax.
I just want to sleep.
Just a minute, please.

senses.head: A moment ago; very recently
examples: I just got home.
She's just left the office.
We just now heard the news.

senses.head: Exactly
examples: That's just what I needed.
He looks just like his father.
The soup is just right.

senses.head: Barely; by a very small amount
examples: We got to the station just in time.
I just missed the bus.

senses.head: Really; absolutely, for emphasis
examples: The view was just amazing.
Just listen to me for a second!

senses.head: Almost, in just about

senses.head: Possibly; perhaps, with might, may or could

entries.русский: только; только что; как раз; едва
entries.type: focusing; also time (just left) and degree (just in time)
entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; before its word in just a minute
entries.form: same spelling as the adjective just (справедливый), but a different word
entries.contrast: American English uses just with the simple past as easily as with the present perfect: I just ate and I've just eaten are both correct. Just now means 'a moment ago' — for Russian прямо сейчас say right now. Justly (group 3) means 'fairly' and comes from the adjective, not from this adverb.

examples: The meeting starts at nine sharp.
Be here at noon sharp or we leave without you.
The store opens at 8 a.m. sharp.
Turn sharp left after the bridge.
The trail bends sharp right at the creek.
The violins were playing slightly sharp.
He tends to sing sharp when he's nervous.

senses.head: Exactly, after a clock time
examples: The meeting starts at nine sharp.
Be here at noon sharp or we leave without you.
The store opens at 8 a.m. sharp.

senses.head: Suddenly and at a steep angle, of turning
examples: Turn sharp left after the bridge.
The trail bends sharp right at the creek.

senses.head: Above the correct pitch, in music
examples: The violins were playing slightly sharp.
He tends to sing sharp when he's nervous.

entries.type: time; also direction (turn sharp left) and manner (sing sharp)
entries.position: after its word — at six sharp; before left or right; end in sing sharp
entries.modifies: clock times; left, right; verbs of singing and playing
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective sharp
entries.contrast: Flat sharp has three narrow uses: clock time (at six sharp), turning (turn sharp left) and music (sing sharp). For 'suddenly, by a lot' or 'harshly' use sharply: Prices rose sharply; she spoke sharply (group 3). Look sharp is British for 'hurry up'; in American English You look sharp is the adjective — you look stylish.

examples: Lie flat on your back and relax.
Store the posters flat, not rolled.
He fell flat on his face.
She ran the mile in five minutes flat.
The crew changed the tires in ten seconds flat.
I'm flat broke until payday.
She turned him down flat.
He flat out lied to me.
His jokes fell flat with the audience.
The new ad campaign fell flat.
She sang a little flat on the high notes.
The trumpets came in flat in the second verse.

senses.head: In a level, horizontal position
examples: Lie flat on your back and relax.
Store the posters flat, not rolled.
He fell flat on his face.

senses.head: Exactly; no more, after a length of time
examples: She ran the mile in five minutes flat.
The crew changed the tires in ten seconds flat.

senses.head: Completely; directly and firmly
examples: I'm flat broke until payday.
She turned him down flat.
He flat out lied to me.

senses.head: Without the effect intended, in fall flat
examples: His jokes fell flat with the audience.
The new ad campaign fell flat.

senses.head: Below the correct pitch, in music
examples: She sang a little flat on the high notes.
The trumpets came in flat in the second verse.

entries.type: manner; also degree (flat broke) and time (ten seconds flat)
entries.position: end — after the verb or a time phrase; before its word in flat broke
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective flat
entries.contrast: Flat flat follows the verb: turned me down flat, lie flat. Flatly goes before the verb and is used for refusing, denying and speaking without emotion: He flatly refused (group 3). Flat out is informal American for 'completely, openly' (He flat out lied) or 'at top speed' (working flat out).

examples: You know full well what I mean.

The ball hit him full in the face.
She looked him full in the eye and said no.

senses.head: Very well; perfectly, in full well
examples: You know full well what I mean.
She knew full well that the check would bounce.

senses.head: Directly; squarely
examples: The ball hit him full in the face.
She looked him full in the eye and said no.

entries.type: degree; also manner (full in the face)
entries.position: before its word — full well; end in hit him full in the face
entries.modifies: well; in the face, in the eye
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective full
entries.contrast: The everyday adverb is fully: fully booked, I fully agree — never I full agree (group 3). Flat full survives only in a few fixed phrases: know full well, full in the face. I'm full (я наелся) is the adjective.

examples: The twins always dress alike.
Great minds think alike.
The teacher treats all her students alike.
The show is popular with kids and adults alike.
Rich and poor alike were hit by the recession.

senses.head: In the same or a very similar way
examples: The twins always dress alike.
Great minds think alike.
The teacher treats all her students alike.

senses.head: Equally; both, after two or more nouns
examples: The show is popular with kids and adults alike.
Rich and poor alike were hit by the recession.

entries.type: manner; also focusing (young and old alike)
entries.position: end — after the verb, or after a pair of nouns
entries.modifies: verbs; pairs of nouns (kids and adults alike)
entries.form: a- word — like alone and asleep, never used before a noun
entries.contrast: Alike never stands before a noun: similar houses, not alike houses. After look or be it is the adjective: The twins look alike. Compare like, a preposition that needs an object: She looks like her mother, but She and her mother look alike.

examples: She has lived alone since her husband died.
I don't like walking home alone at night.
You shouldn't try to move that couch alone.
You alone can make that decision.
Money alone won't solve the problem.
In July alone, the company hired 300 people.

senses.head: Without other people
examples: She has lived alone since her husband died.
I don't like walking home alone at night.
You shouldn't try to move that couch alone.

senses.head: Only; and nobody or nothing else, after a noun or pronoun
examples: You alone can make that decision.
Money alone won't solve the problem.
In July alone, the company hired 300 people.

entries.position: end — live alone; after its word in you alone, money alone
entries.form: a- word — never used before a noun (a lone rider, a lonely house)
entries.contrast: Alone means 'without other people' with no feeling attached; lonely is an adjective meaning 'sad because you are alone': I live alone, but I'm not lonely. Leave me alone = оставь меня в покое. Let alone (не говоря уже о) links two phrases: He can't boil an egg, let alone cook dinner.
